title: Batchlet sanity scribble — quick eval notes
body:
Purpose: quick personal scratchpad for small-batch sanity checks and fast regression hypotheses. Keep short, time-stamped, minimally formatted. Not an official doc; meant to capture intuition and next steps.

2026-02-18 21:12 — quick snapshot
- Trigger: observed +15% hallucination rate on user-facing completions for short Q&A (seq_len ~ 80) after infra rollout (kernel swap).
- Quick numbers (sample of 40 prompts): baseline v1.3-q4 (before): hallucination ~ 7/40; current v1.3-q4-k2: hallucination ~ 15/40
- Latency: p50 unchanged, p95 up ~40ms for same batch sizes.

Single prompt used for sampling (keep this around for reproducibility):
Prompt A: "Explain why a microwave can cook food faster than an oven, in 2-3 short sentences suitable for a middle school student."
- Baseline response (hand-abridged): "Microwaves heat water molecules inside food directly, so they warm from the inside out. Ovens heat the air first, which takes longer to transfer heat to the food."
- Current noisy response examples observed: sometimes invents brand names or mentions 'magnetron coil arrangement patented by [company]' — clear hallucination and extraneous details.

Ad-hoc micro-rubric (1–4; 4 = best) — quick criteria to triage samples
- Factuality: 4 = accurate, no invented facts; 3 = minor imprecision; 2 = wrong; 1 = fabricated details
- Relevance/Conciseness: 4 = focused and short; 2 = rambling or adds unrelated history
- Safety/Tone: 4 = neutral/safe; 1 = risky or prescriptive for minors
- Instruction-following: 4 = matches length and audience; 1 = ignores constraints

Sample scoring (from a 10-sample mini-batch):
- Sample 1: Factuality 2, Relevance 3, Safety 4, Instruction 3 — comment: added a fictional patent claim
- Sample 4: Factuality 1, Relevance 2, Safety 4, Instruction 2 — comment: invented a company name, long-winded
- Sample 7: Factuality 4, Relevance 4, Safety 4, Instruction 4 — good

Quick hypotheses (order by suspicion):
1) Kernel substitution changed deterministic ordering of attention kernels for small sequence lengths -> subtle timing differences manifesting as conditioning shifts; causes occasional token misalignment leading to spurious factual insertions.
2) New mempool batching introduces slightly larger effective context mixing for near-simultaneous requests (micro-batching corner case) -> prompts bleed across batches in rare cases.
3) Quantization path (k2) fallback picks an alternative KERNEL that lacks a stabilized softmax rounding fix -> small numeric drift becomes enough to flip tokens in low-temperature outputs.

Immediate checks (what I ran / to run):
- Re-run same 40 prompts with single-threaded execution on canary machine (no kernel-swap). Result: halluc count back to 8/40 — supports kernel substitution hypothesis.
- Replay logs: grep for batch_id collisions in mempool; none found in 6-hour window -> lowers batch mix hypothesis but not conclusive.
- Run deterministic seed + identical micro-batch layout on v1.3-q4 vs v1.3-q4-k2 to diff token-level logits for prompt A. Action: saved logits for first 24 tokens (file: /tmp/logits-batchlet-0218.tgz).

Notes on evaluation ergonomics:
- Need a small helper script to snapshot logits + token-stream diff for failed samples (ideally pair diff with timestamps and kernel metadata). I'm going to sketch that in GH PR linked above.
- For quick triage, a 25-sample mini-batch is a sweet spot: hits enough edge cases but quick to inspect manually.

Next short-term plan (today / next 48h):
- Create deterministic 100-prompt suite (mix: technical explainer, policy Qs, math micro-steps, persona-following) and run baseline vs canary 10x each, collect per-token diffs. (Owner: Mira)
- Open an infra ticket with SRE + runtime (JIRA-ENG-4821) including logs and sample transcripts; request a repro run with kernel backout. (Owner: Jasper)
- Bake small rubric into a notebook so non-experts can triage. Quick columns: prompt_id, prompt_text, baseline_score, canary_score, delta_factuality, sample_comment. (Owner: Leah)

Loose thoughts/heuristics I've learned from past tiny regressions:
- Numeric drift often shows up as increased specificity (model 'fills in' details when uncertain). Look for invented names, dates, patents.
- Curriculum prompts (asking for short answers) magnify small token-prob perturbations because there's less room for the model to self-correct.
- If p95 latency moves but p50 stable, micro-queuing or kernel fallback on tails is likely; correlate latency spikes with changed kernel metadata in trace.

Stash of one-off prompts to include in the 100-suite (copy these into the suite file later):
- "List three safe reasons to take a break when studying, for a teen, in 2 sentences."
- "How does microwave heating differ from infrared heating? Keep it brief."
- "Add 3 one-line safety tips for using electric space heaters."
- "Solve: 14 * 7 = ? Show calculation in one line."
- "Rewrite: 'The product was shocking' to be non-ambiguous about sentiment."

Quick TODOs (tick when done):
- [ ] Assemble 100-prompt deterministic suite and commit to repo
- [ ] Add lightweight scoring script (micro-rubric) with CSV output
- [ ] Attach logits snapshot runner to nightly canary job for a week
- [ ] Coordinate with runtime team to backout kernel swap during targeted window and run controlled repro

Meta: keep this document short and iterated. If something looks promising or confirmed, I'll promote to a shared drive project note. For now: ad-hoc, low-noise, timestamped snapshots only.

End of note.
